speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to read the Orders of the Day.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our construction industry continues to face significant headwinds due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: While most construction work has resumed since August last year, the inflow of migrant workers who form the main bulk of the workforce has remained constrained due to the global impact of the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have recently tightened our border control measures with a number of countries, including Bangladesh and India, which are our main sources of construction Work Permit holders.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: While this was necessary to safeguard public health, it has made the shortage of manpower in the sector even more severe.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In tandem, construction manpower costs have been rising.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This has affected both new as well as on-going projects.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have also implemented various Safe Management Measures to keep workers safe and reduce the risk of COVID-19 transmission.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These are important public health precautions, but they also inevitably impact productivity.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This, together with the on-going manpower shortage, has, unfortunately, led to project delays.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Barring any unforeseen circumstances, we are expecting a further delay of three months, arising from the recent border measures.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are faced with a difficult balancing act – the more we need to tighten border measures for everyone’s safety, the greater the impact will be on construction timelines, on projects and on home buyers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We had, therefore, intervened significantly since last year to assist the many stakeholders across the value chain that have been affected by rising costs and delays.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For construction firms, we introduced a $1.36 billion Construction Support Package last year to help our contractors bear part of the additional costs they had to incur due to construction delays and Safe Management Measures.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We had also assisted firms with Foreign Worker Levy rebates and waivers, as well as wage subsidies via the Jobs Support Scheme or JSS, to relieve some of their burden from manpower costs and help keep local jobs.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Under Part 8 of the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act (COTMA), we established a mechanism for firms to seek relief from additional rental costs that are incurred due to construction delays caused by COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And under Parts 8A and 8B of COTMA, we legislated a universal extension of time of four months and mandated the sharing of non-manpower prolongation costs between project parties.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For developers, we had earlier provided a 12-month extension of the Project Completion Period and Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty remission timelines for completion, to account for delays due to COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Part 8C of COTMA will also allow developers whose projects face construction delays to seek relief on the date of delivery of possession.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For home buyers, Part 2 of COTMA prohibits developers from withholding or forfeiting any part of the booking fee paid by home buyers under the Option to Purchase during the relief period, or terminating agreements for sale and purchase of the property because the home buyer was not able to make payment.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We also capped the late payment interest and charges under agreements for sale and purchase of property, to protect home buyers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In addition, under Part 8C of COTMA, where the developer has extended the delivery date, home buyers may also seek reimbursement from the developer, up to a specified cap, if they incur certain out-of-pocket expenses due to a delay in delivery of the unit by the developer.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For HDB flat buyers, HDB has been progressively updating home buyers who have been affected, on the revised completion dates.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For those who are unable to make alternative housing arrangements, HDB has assisted them with Interim Rental Housing flats.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Now, the manpower situation will be further exacerbated by the recent tightening of our border measures with Bangladesh, India and other countries.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As both Ministers Lawrence Wong and Gan Kim Yong have explained earlier today, we have to tighten our border controls to better protect Singapore from heightened COVID-19 risks.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And we should expect these stringent measures to be in place for some time, given the worsening situation overseas.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In response, we have recently announced more support measures to help the construction industry.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, we have granted an additional 49-day Extension of Time (EOT) for eligible public sector construction projects, on top of the 122 days or four months of EOT already provided under COTMA last year on a universal basis.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This gives contractors more time to complete their projects.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Second, contractors working on eligible public sector projects with an awarded contract sum of up to $100 million will receive 0.1% of their awarded contract sum for every month of delay as payment for non-manpower related qualifying costs under COTMA.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: There is no need to provide further detailed substantiation for their claims.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Measures such as these will help firms to cope.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This will allow firms to continue bringing in workers for their projects even though some Chinese Overseas Training Centres had halted operations due to the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In addition, we have been proactively working with industry associations and firms to explore other ways to resume the inflow of construction Work Permit holders from other source countries safely.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will continue to work with them on additional measures to help alleviate the tight labour situation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In January this year, we had also set up a task force, led by BCA and comprising Government agencies, consultants, as well as trade and professional associations representing developers, contractors, quantity surveyors and architects.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The task force is studying how to enhance our standard construction procurement contracts in both the public and the private sectors to mitigate the impact of the current pandemic as well as future crises.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, we have received feedback that contractors have been buffering for risks in their current tender bids for uncertainty, which has resulted in an increase in tender prices for new contracts.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is understandable as they are worried about unanticipated cost increases due to unexpected developments, twists and turns, during the course of the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our new construction contracts ought to enable more equitable risk and cost sharing during pandemic events and crises of this nature.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Everyone along the value chain will need to step up and share the burden of uncertainty and help one another get through these challenging times together.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is to ensure that no one single stakeholder group in the construction industry bears a disproportionate share of the burden imposed by COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Clause 3 of the Bill introduces a new Part 10A to COTMA.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This provides a relief framework that will allow parties, such as contractors, to apply to adjust the contract sum for their projects, to take into account increases in foreign manpower cost due to COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The new section 79B defines the scope of the contracts covered by this framework.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, it will apply to contracts for construction works.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These are contracts of longer duration that generally involve structural works and are most likely to be affected by the foreign manpower crunch.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Second, it will apply to construction contracts entered into before 1 October 2020.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Parties may not have fully priced in foreign manpower cost increases before this date, as there had been substantial Foreign Worker Levy waivers and rebates provided by the Government up to that point.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And third, it excludes contracts that have been completed or terminated.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It also makes clear that the purpose of the adjustment is to take into consideration the increasing foreign manpower costs of Work Permit holders incurred due to COVID-19 during the relief period.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Additionally, it states that a party must have made a reasonable attempt to negotiate a contract sum adjustment with the other party, before he can apply for an Assessor to determine the adjustment.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Construction projects involve many parties, often in long interlocking contractual value chains, and if one goes down, the entire project may be put at risk.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Moreover, many of the developers and contractors in the construction sector have long-term relationships.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At the end of the day, all stakeholders are part of the same built environment eco-system and, on a project, all parties seek to deliver on that project.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And for this eco-system to thrive and grow, stakeholders need to step up to help one another during these challenging times.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We encourage all parties affected by the pandemic to negotiate with each other in good faith, before triggering the adjudicatory process set out in this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have, anecdotally, seen such "give and take" in the sector already.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, some developers we know have given their contractors an extension of time beyond what had been mandated in the existing COTMA for the completion of on-going projects.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Some have also provided advanced payments and increased the frequency of progress payments to aid contractors’ cashflow and to keep projects going.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The new Division 2 of the Bill sets out the processes of the relief framework.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Section 79F details how a party can apply for an adjustment to the contract sum.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, parties who wish to seek relief must apply to the Registrar to appoint an Assessor who can then determine the adjustment.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The new section 79G explains how an Assessor will determine an adjustment.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, the Assessor must seek to achieve an outcome that is just and equitable in the circumstances of the case.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Assessor must also consider matters and principles that will be prescribed in the subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, in arriving at a just and equitable decision, the Assessor should take into account all the facts, including the loss suffered or benefit obtained by any contractual party, such as levy rebates.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: (In Mandarin):    To prevent COVID-19 from spreading and to safeguard public health, the Government has to strengthen border controls.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Because of that, the construction industry is facing a very severe foreign manpower shortage.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Government has already put in place various measures to address the manpower shortage and to support construction firms.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These include the recent increase in Foreign Worker Levy rebate and further extension of time for eligible public sector construction projects.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At the same time, we are aware that there is a need to provide support for existing construction contracts where parties may not have adequately priced in this unexpected increase in foreign manpower cost for their construction works.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: An assessor will examine each case and determine whether the contract sum needs to be increased.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: However, contractors must first try to negotiate with their clients before applying for this relief.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I call upon all parties to negotiate in good faith before triggering this process.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: (In English): Madam, I have spoken about many of the measures that the Government has implemented to support our construction industry through this pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But the reality is that these are just stop-gap measures to try to staunch some of the bleeding.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They are not sustainable in the long run.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That is why we want to work with the construction industry to press on with on-going efforts to transform the sector and accelerate the pace of change, even as we put in place measures to support the industry during these difficult times.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This latest disruption in inflow of migrant workers has shown how vulnerable the construction industry is, because of our over-reliance on low-cost migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We must build greater resilience in our sector, create more good, productive local jobs and move decisively away from manpower-intensive construction methods.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have already started this transformation some time back, with the launch of the Construction Industry Transformation Map in 2017.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At MND's Committee of Supply debate in March this year, we had announced a suite of initiatives to partner the industry in accelerating the pace of transformation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, we will adopt a value chain approach to drive transformation through the new Growth and Transformation Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The scheme recognises that the construction industry works through value chains.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It will, therefore, support alliances of firms all along the value chain, from developers and consultants to builders and contractors.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Each alliance will develop a business plan to achieve ambitious outcomes in productivity and digitalisation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This would be through the use of productive methods of construction, including Design for Manufacturing and Assembly (DfMA), and technology, such as Integrated Digital Delivery, or IDD, as well as efforts to enhance sustainability, workforce development, including the creation of local jobs, business growth and strategic collaboration.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This will support our industry in its recovery from COVID-19 and help our firms minimise disruptions to their operations by leveraging DfMA and IDD technologies and other innovative, productive processes.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In addition, we will review our foreign manpower levers for the construction sector.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are also studying the reduction of the construction Dependency Ratio Ceiling, or DRC, to support more manpower-lean construction.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will continue to consult our industry partners before making any major moves.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This Bill will facilitate more equitable sharing of the increase in foreign manpower costs brought about by COVID-19 amongst parties to existing contracts.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Taken together with our other measures, it will help alleviate the significant stresses that the construction industry is currently facing due to the manpower crunch.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But even as we deal with these near-term challenges, we must keep our eyes on the future.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will continue to work with the industry to quicken the pace of transformation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These structural changes will be painful, but they are necessary to ensure that the industry as a whole can emerge more resilient and more productive from this crisis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a real concern for the sector.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: According to some construction bosses, even as the Government has rolled out a number of assistance schemes and levy waiver since the onset of COVID-19, the situation, especially for smaller sub-contractors, has been difficult, disruptive and, for some, even desperate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And some are at the risk of going out-of-business.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Earlier on during Question Time today, I spoke of the difficulty of securing entry passes for their foreign workers for many contractors prior to the latest spike in the COVID-19 cases, resulting in significant operational unpredictability.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I asked the Second Minister for Manpower about reimbursement of IPA fees and opening up more non-traditional source countries from where foreign workers can be recruited from as a way to moderate the impact of COVID-19 on businesses in this sector.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note that this Bill will cover contracts to build residential units, including existing contracts to build HDB BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister confirm how any adjustment in the price of HDB contracts with builders would impact home buyers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would they be at risk of upward price adjustments?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, many public sector projects would also see a hike in construction costs arising from this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the same vein, I would like to ask the Minister what this would amount to and its impact on the Government's Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, has the Ministry considered the impact of the Bill on Town Councils and whether it would be providing assistance to them?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Earlier this year, the Minister, at a seminar organised by BCA and REDAS, confirmed that construction contracts for the built environment sector are expected to grow to between $23 billion and $28 billion in 2021 as the sector recovers from the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This was up from the $21.3 billion worth of projects awarded in 2020, even as that figure fell by $10 billion owing to the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, rewriting a contract price to one that was not initially agreed to by the parties is a drastic intervention that must be exercised with utmost care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The construction industry has a significant impact on our economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry consider cutting the foreign worker levy?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, I am told that the cost of employing a general worker is now $150 per day and a tiler is now $250 per day.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the current labour crunch, one can foresee staff poaching between companies, which would invariably add on to the cost.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government consider more measures to help contractors to meet their higher overheads?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be a further review to assist the industry?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second is to give contractors more breathing space on their project completion schedule.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Currently, workers are subject to many screening measures and movement restrictions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: All these measures affect work planning and execution, quite apart from the impact on the workers' morale, many of whom are already stressed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, contractors are facing a candle that is burning on both ends.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, we hope that the Ministry can get the buy-in of developers and Government agencies, to understand the difficulties faced by the construction companies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Contractors are just as anxious to get their jobs completed, as are the developers and the various Government agencies overseeing public projects.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The closure of travel from the traditional labour markets is like denying water supply to runners taking part in an endurance race in the desert.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Government agencies are using the BCA template and agencies are pressing the contractors to meet their deadlines.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is almost oblivious of the dilemma facing the construction industry.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There has to be a coordinated approach to this whole problem, besides just giving financial support to contractors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These agencies managing public projects must also review their contract terms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wish to offer just three brief points of intervention.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The first two are of a more practical nature about the scope of coverage for this set of amendments and whether there are better ways to design our labour exchange.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The third point is of a more fundamental nature about the productivity, or lack thereof, in our construction industry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, while I understand that the construction sector has been the most severely affected by the COVID-19 restrictions and that construction projects tend to be the sort where cost projections can be most rapidly invalidated by changing conditions, one is, nevertheless, left to wonder why other sectors with large numbers of non-traditional source (NTS) workers were not included in the scope for contract renegotiation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, in operating our Town Councils, we are also aware of the heavy reliance of our contractors on NTS workers in our conservancy operations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Agri-tech and certain process industries also rely relatively heavily on foreign worker inflows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, and relatedly, I am wondering about the current efforts of this Government to ease the reallocation of workers already in Singapore between firms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: During the round-up speech on the previous set of amendments to the Bill, Minister of State Tan Kiat How referred to the establishment of a SCAL Construction Manpower Exchange or SCMX, meant to ease the transition of workers from one employer to the next.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I fully support this idea; not least because it promotes greater efficiency, but also because it serves to further alleviate the risk of the need to constantly introduce new workers, some of whom may inadvertently harbour the virus even after serving the necessary quarantine protocols, as we have seen demonstrated in recent times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wonder if the Ministry would be willing to share an update first on the status of the SCMX thus far.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Ultimately, my concerns are about the success of the SCMX in practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Employers who subsequently lose contracts may see a competitive reason to send their workers back, rather than avail them to the exchange.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thus, while they may well save on repatriation costs if they were to relinquish their workers, firms may feel that not releasing their NTS workers could damage their competitors' viability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And the threat of doing so may further favour their own position as incumbents since only they have a guaranteed pool of workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While workers may easily request a transfer at the moment as long as they have the employer's agreement between the 40th and 21st day prior to the expiry of their permit, some employers could simply choose to renew the permit first, then subsequently cancel the permit less than three weeks prior to the original end date.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Anecdotally, we have received feedback that such practices are far from uncommon.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am left to wonder if the Ministry has considered how to better refine the system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Ministry can then play the role of match-maker, absorbing workers into a roster.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The firm giving up workers will place their repatriation costs into an escrow account to be managed by the Ministry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These funds, net of costs for those workers who wish to be returned home, will be released to the firm if another company subsequently hires the workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hiring companies, in lieu of paying for the search, travel and quarantine costs of new workers, can instead be tasked with financing the short-term room and board for in-situ workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My third point, Mdm Deputy Speaker, concerns the construction sector in general.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is well-known that for the productivity challenges that we have faced in our economy, the construction sector has been even worse off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While some have objected to this characterisation, most observers, including reports issued by academia, policy-makers and even the industry itself, have recognised how the sector lags in terms of productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The justifications have been varied: from purported low skills of workers, especially related to a large transient foreign worker pool, to inadequate project planning, to inadequate mechanisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One common theme runs through these many explanations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And it is simply this: with steady access to a large pool of foreign construction workers, most paid at very low wages, it is unsurprising that firms rationally choose to substitute capital with labour, and skilled workers with unskilled ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will go on as long as it is cheaper to bring in two or three low-cost workers to do the job of one higher skilled but undeniably more costly worker.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While one may simply argue that this reflects marginal cost calculations on the part of construction firms, this practice is, ultimately, to the detriment of more than just productivity per se.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Beyond these points of caution, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I have no objections to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We empathise with the difficulties faced by our contractors who have been severely ravaged by the COVID-19 pandemic but there are also other considerations to be made before we can support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First and foremost, who is going to pay for the financial relief?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, with the surging property market now, the property developer can easily pass on the increased cost to the property buyers, many of whom are Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this happens, we will be imposing another indirect tax on our people who are already suffering under the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The way to prevent this is to, first, dampen the bullish sentiment in the property market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Reining in property prices is what we need to do now in order not to exacerbate the social inequality in our country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this way, foreigners and property developers who may have to lower prices to retain buying interest will be the ultimate payers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government may also not want the contractors to sit on their laurels after the new measures kick in.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government can integrate the relief measures into the built environment sector strategy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is also a great opportunity to attract some of our Singaporeans to rejoin the construction sector because contractors can now pay higher wages as the wages of migrant workers have shot up significantly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the Government has so far not taken any initiative to encourage this, as far as I know.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this way, we can also tackle another problem and, that is, maintaining our family formation rate and total fertility rate, preventing a COVID-19 gap in our future population structure, which may become another problem in the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is defeatist in a sense because we are succumbing to the effect of a migrant worker shortage, inflicting damage to our contractors and then worsening the housing shortage, which directly impact our lives.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, this need not be the case if we are prepared to bear with short-term inconveniences to shake ourselves off the addictive reliance on foreign labour with the right policies over time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we increase the ABSD, restricting the number of migrant workers will not worsen livelihoods that much.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, our contractors will have more time to adjust to a new supply chain and may increase employment of our local workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our young Singaporean couples get their rental flats and all these, paid by the foreign buyers of our local properties.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   	Mdm Deputy Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to provide financial assistance to help local construction companies and contractors pay for the increase in wage costs incurred as a result of the further tightening of foreign workers coming into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We sympathise with the difficulties faced by our contractors, who have been severely affected by the pandemic, but there are other issues to be considered before we support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, and most importantly, who will pay for this financial relief?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: According to the Bill, an independent assessor will be appointed to assess the increase in the cost of foreign workers due to the tightening of the foreign labour market, and the assessed cost will be borne by the developers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, with the current surge in property prices, it will be easy for developers to pass on the increased cost to buyers, many of whom are Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this happens, it will be equivalent to an additional indirect tax.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The way to prevent this from happening is, first of all, to curb optimism in the property market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Curbing property prices is also what we need to do now to avoid exacerbating social inequality.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, Singaporeans, especially young couples planning to start a family, are facing a housing shortage.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, it is a good policy to control excessive buying from foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, the appropriate solution is to increase the ABSD to reduce the demand from foreigners, curb the property market and use the collected ABSD to pay for the financial assistance to contractors.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this way, foreigners and property developers will be the ones who, ultimately, foot the bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, the Government may not want contractors to be just enjoying the cake.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current problem is that contractors have long relied on foreign workers, so we have to urge them to speed up the re-design and automation of their work processes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the Government has not taken any actions to encourage such development.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, if we apply the right policies, this may not necessarily be the case.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the contrary, contractors will have more time to adapt to the new supply chain and increase the employment opportunities of local workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, young Singaporean couples can be allocated housing, which is paid for by foreigners and property buyers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In English): This view is one more opportunity for us to reaffirm our confidence that Singapore can survive and do better with a different economic model.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will help contractors cope with the increased manpower costs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, as raised in my previous speech on the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) (Amendment No 2) Bill, it remains unclear whether yet again allowing modifications of agreed-upon contracts is a lasting solution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, we are talking about labour supply problems that may be long run, given that the pandemic shows no signs of abating in many developing countries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On that, I have three points of clarifications.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is about temporarily allowing workers to get their skills certified here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Typically, migrant workers looking to join our construction sector must first enrol in Overseas Testing Centres (OTCs) within their home countries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At these OTCs, they must complete either the Skills Evaluation Certificate (SEC) or Skills Evaluation Certificate (Knowledge) (SEC(K)), which certify that the worker qualifies as Basic-Skilled construction workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This reduces the bottleneck in China, where some OTCs remain closed, and helps alleviate our labour supply crunch.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify what is the usual passing rate of the SEC and SEC(K) tests in each country’s OTCs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For areas where the passing rate is usually quite high, can the Government consider introducing similar temporary exemptions from other source countries?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, there remain OTCs that are closed in Myanmar and Thailand.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This can help to temporarily alleviate the supply crunch without compromising on the skill requirements we have set.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is about expanding the list of source countries which we debated earlier.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have always restricted the list of countries from which each industry can hire Work Pass holders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For the construction sector, the list is Malaysia, China, India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Philippines, Thailand, Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan and South Korea.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government explain the basis for restricting this list of source countries?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government also consider expanding the list of source countries?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are likely other countries where migrant workers with basic skills can be found.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, times like this highlight the risks of over-relying on a limited number of source countries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With a more diverse supply pool, it might become easier to find higher skilled workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We then could move towards raising our skills requirements for what counts as Basic Skilled or Higher Skilled, as well as tapering off the number of lower skilled migrant workers in the sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is about the impact on Government expenses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I understand that the final impact will have to be quantified by Assessors, who will have to look at applications on a case-by-case basis, has the Government at least estimated the range of increased costs that it will have to bear as a result of potential contract adjustments?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is likely that, at any given time, the Government is the largest spender on construction contracts in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must help the construction sector but we must also find the balance and guard against the possibility that all of our yet-to-complete projects see ballooning costs as a result of this legislative amendment.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In confronting the new challenges facing our country with the new clusters of community cases in recent weeks, it is important that we and members of the public avoid false dichotomies.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, we must avoid the false dichotomy that in formulating policy, we have to choose between one of only two options: either close borders to save lives or open borders to save the economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The presumption is that we should prioritise human well-being at some cost to the economy, so that keeping the borders open is tantamount to choosing to place the economy above human lives.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In reality, closing the borders also imposes costs on human well-being, a point I think that has been made by several people, but let us think about that.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Stricter border controls that make it more difficult to obtain the help of foreign domestic workers to take care of our elderly citizens, for example, reduce our senior citizens' well-being.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Restricting the entry of foreign workers from certain countries with high incidence of COVID-19 infections would delay the completion of many construction projects, including BTO flats.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This would have an impact on plans for starting a family for many people.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Companies that have a high reliance on foreign workers might go out of business which would cause citizen workers their jobs as well.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The loss of jobs means not only a loss of income but also imposes costs on the well-being of the retrenched workers and their family members.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Increasing the quarantine period from 14 days to 21 days for international travellers except for those from a few countries with lower infection rates, provides some degree of safety for our citizens.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, even then, the economy will not benefit fully from international economic integration as it did during the pre-COVID-19 days.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Instead of thinking about binary choices, like whether to keep borders closed or open, our policy has to adapt to unforeseen circumstances that the evolving pandemic presents to us by improving trade-offs.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The circuit breaker introduced last year shut down non-essential businesses in order to limit the spread of the virus.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The adoption of measures like safe distancing and the mandatory wearing of masks helped to reduce the crucial parameter known as the reproduction rate – the parameter that gives the number of people an infectious person will infect over the whole course of their disease in a fully susceptible population.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Those measures help to improve the trade-off so that, for a given level of protection of health, more business activity could resume.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: When the number of community cases is successfully brought down, opening up our borders risks importing cases of infected persons.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: While testing and imposing quarantine orders on foreigners help to reduce the risk of community spread caused by imported cases, implementing travel bubbles requires both countries to have effective national control of the pandemic.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Restricting entry of foreign workers from countries with a high incidence of COVID-19 infections and turning to alternative sources with lower infection rates seek to undo the adverse shift in trade-off to some degree.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Source countries might also impose travel restrictions on their own citizens travelling to Singapore, which require Singapore-based firms to look elsewhere for workers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, turning to alternative sources of foreign workers has business consequences as wage costs might increase, which this Bill seeks to address.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, there are inevitable costs that will have to be borne with the spike of new cases in several parts of the world even as we seek to achieve what we regard as an optimal trade-off.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In view of this, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our built sector is facing intense pressure on three fronts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One, the number of construction workers in the built sector continues to shrink.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Among projects, there are uneven manpower availability among different layers of contractors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Post-COVID-19 projects, given higher margin, are able to marshal more manpower resources.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The majority in the construction industry, I must say, understand the need for the recent curbs on new inflow of migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Nevertheless, the reality is that the manpower shortage will only get worse in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two, the industry is experiencing a surge in construction materials pricing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As of now, the strongest companies – those with a good number of post-COVID-19 projects, high margins and sizeable reserves – are able to get adequate financing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, most companies are struggling to get financing from banks.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Based on industry feedback, a number of them, I was told, are resorting to tapping on financing companies and are paying financing costs of around 10%.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In view of these three sets of challenges, MND’s recent announcements are very much welcomed by the industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Second, increasing the length of time for projects will help because, for some projects, they can wait out the current spike in material cost, as well as the sizeable manpower shortage.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Three, easing of restrictions on Chinese workers is helpful.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, I do want to caution that beyond the large Chinese construction companies, many local construction companies may not have the links to recruit sufficient Chinese manpower given the current shortage of construction workers in China.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And the salaries of Chinese workers in the construction sector are two to three times more expensive than those from the Indian subcontinent.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And it is not easy to persuade Chinese workers to do the full range of jobs, even if we can persuade them to come to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Beyond the measures announced today, I hope that MND can continue to pre-empt this unfolding industry crisis.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For example, it may not be possible for us to bring in migrant workers from the Indian subcontinent for many months, or even beyond a year's time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And even if we want to diversify the source of migrant workers from the rest of developing Asia, it is also very difficult to predict whether those countries will see a surge in infection that we see in India.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must also plan the possibility of another circuit breaker, should community spread become more prevalent in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Over the past few weeks, I have been working with the built sector to come up with some proposals that can form our contingency plan, should the situation deteriorate significantly.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One, we can introduce more short-term measures to better utilise our existing workers in the sector.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For example, we can temporarily increase the allowable age for migrant workers to stay in Singapore from 50 to 55 years old, and to potentially up to 60 years old with regular medical reviews.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There are many different kinds of jobs, some are not as strenuous as others.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Let us trust that our companies can strike the right balance, as we increase the age in the short run.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Another possibility is to get the construction companies and safety community to explore urgent and temporary measures to increase the allowable man-hours.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Based on industry feedback, the work intensity in many sites have reduced due to increased delays in material arrival and decreased subcontractor productivity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For selected work sites, can workers be given the option of working during their off-days, if it is clear that they have more rest during the normal days, due to decreased work intensity?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Of course, these proposals must be carefully considered and implemented, but we are in a crisis and we need to explore all options.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two, we must urgently explore new sources of manpower.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many of us agree that the situation in India is extremely dire and it could take a while to sort out.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But we must diversify and explore other countries, knowing fully well that we cannot predict which sources will eventually come through for us.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As such, could the Government consider new sources of migrant construction workers, such as Cambodia, Laos, even the Riau Islands in Indonesia?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Beyond the new sources, we must also ensure that migrant workers are free of COVID-19 when they come to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, is it possible for the Government to work with the built sector to set up and operate processing and quarantine centres in these countries?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This will ensure that testing is done by trusted vendors, perhaps even using our own test kits.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The facilities and cleanliness operations are managed by our stringent standards.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Workers can use dedicated transport, operated by us, to come to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And upon arrival, we can test again and vaccinate the workers immediately, while they undergo further quarantine.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It will take us a while to get this going and some of these sources, even after we invest time and effort, may not work out.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, I hope that our Government can actively pursue various options as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Of course, the planning part of the project can go through, but we must reduce construction demand when we have a vastly reduced manpower supply, or the excess demand will lead to unnecessary cost surge.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Five, we can prepare for a different implementation of circuit breakers for the built sector.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: COVID-19 in the dormitories is still largely contained, there is a successful segregation between the construction sector from the rest of Singapore, and we are able to do more frequent and extensive testing in the construction sector.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As such, the industry hopes that the Government can allow as much work to continue, even during a circuit breaker, by ensuring that the construction sites remain as air-tight as possible.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A lot of hard work will be required to come up with a revised circuit breaker plan that is tailor-fitted to the present circumstances.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I hope that we can start preparing for it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Six, monitoring the credit flow to the built sector very carefully.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The Government has done more than its fair share for the built sector.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Nevertheless, Government support will not be sufficient unless the banks and financial institutions do their part to provide sufficient credit.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Seven, consider a further extension to developers on ABSD.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Currently, developers have up to five years from the start of the project to the handover to the buyers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Relieving pressure on the developers will allow them to do more to share the financial pain of the building contractors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Lastly, I would like to suggest that MND and BCA bring on additional staff, or to outsource some of the coordination work.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In my interactions with MND and BCA staff, I note that many of them are trying their best to help the industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But there is just so much more coordination work ahead.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As such, I hope we can beef up the staffing level at the MND family level, just as we have done so decisively at MOM.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: COVID-19 has brought upon an existential threat to the built sector.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Decisive and effective Government action has put off the worst outcome for the industry and the additional measures announced are very much needed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Should the situation confronting the built sector continue to worsen, I hope the Government can actively consider some of the proposals that are mentioned today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With that, I stand in full support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng was concerned about public sector expenditure and about fiscal prudence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The pandemic has, indeed, driven up manpower costs for contractors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we need to share some of this burden.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But in doing so, I agree with him that agencies will need to maintain fiscal discipline.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng spoke about the need to engage developers and contractors to better understand their difficulties and not just press them to complete their projects as if it was business as usual.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And he had given some examples he heard anecdotally about the agencies using a template to press contractors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I seek the Member's support to provide specific details so that we can look into these concerns that have been raised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Based on what we know so far, the only template our agencies had been circulating to contractors is one with regard to prolongation cost submissions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, the agencies are pressing the contractors to submit their claims for prolongation costs, because these agencies want to lean forward to help these firms cope with the non-manpower related cost increases in these projects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, perhaps, for us to check the facts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But I do agree with the Member that we need to adopt an even stronger collaborative posture during this crisis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I have said during the opening speech, at this time in the sector, where there are many interlocking relationships of many stakeholders, if one goes down, the entire project is in peril, and we all have to lean forward and help one another.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This applies to both Government agencies as well as private developers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, when the crisis started last year and construction work had to be shut down for some months, we formed a working group comprising Government agencies and trade associations like SCAL and REDAS.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the start, we met every day digitally, then on a weekly basis; and now, we still meet once a month to better understand the situation on the ground, the dynamic situation, as it evolves, to flag issues up and to work together to resolve them practically.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have also asked Government agencies to lean forward to help contractors through this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Several agencies have gone above and beyond our previously announced measures to help contractors, such as granting even more extensions for contractors to complete their projects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Notwithstanding this, we are looking at ways to simplify the process for public sector projects, similar to what we have done for the non-manpower prolongation cost claims, as well as the additional extensions of time, where direct disbursements and extensions were given respectively, without the need for extensive or prolonged negotiation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to monitor the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on various stakeholders, including developers, and take further steps as necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng referred to BCA’s recently announced scheme to temporarily allow new China construction Work Permit holders to enter Singapore to work first, and then, take their skills certification test locally, instead of in China.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He asked if the Government could consider introducing similar temporary exemptions for other countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To provide some context, BCA had earlier consulted the industry on possible measures to help alleviate the manpower crunch in the construction sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: SCAL, the contractors association, had suggested exercising flexibility on the skills entry requirements, in particular for PRC Work Permit holders, as they are highly skilled in key trades, such as carpentry and structural works, as compared to workers from other countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Henry Kwek asked whether the Government can consider new sources from which to recruit construction Work Permit holders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are prepared to consider various options to alleviate the current manpower crunch facing the whole sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we must consider the COVID-19 situation in these countries, as well as the construction industry’s demand for workers from such sources.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Adding more sources may not necessarily be the solution, as the pandemic seems to be worsening globally.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Regarding Mr Henry Kwek’s suggestion to set up forward operating bases, BCA is actively in discussion with trade associations and industry partners who are exploring upstream ways to ensure the health and safety of the foreign workers that they recruit, while meeting Singapore’s more stringent public health stance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In addition, Mr Kwek suggested increasing the allowable age for foreign workers from 50 to 55, and to 60 with regular medical reviews.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He also asked whether workers can be allowed to work longer if they can have more rest due to the decreased work intensity during weekdays.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Extending working hours beyond this could lead to fatigue and compromise workers’ safety.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Moreover, we all know they have been through an extremely difficult time last year and, still, they are subject to stringent safe management measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Kwek also suggested postponing the construction phase of new projects, given the reduced supply of manpower.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is, indeed, something we are looking into for public sector projects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We need to deliver homes and infrastructure, such as public transport.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we also want to ensure that there is a pipeline of work for our construction sector, so that we retain capacity during this crisis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Kwek also rightly pointed out that we need to prepare for potential further restrictions on construction works, given the fluidity of the current COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I also thank the Member for acknowledging the hard work put in by our officers in helping the industry through this crisis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It has been a difficult time for them and also for the sector as a whole.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will certainly continue to support and encourage our officers as they persevere with these efforts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will take this opportunity to address the query by the Leader of the Opposition about the impact of the COTMA amendment Bill on BTO prices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Bill relates to construction contracts before October 2020; so existing contracts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And those BTOs that have already been sold are already sold.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Likewise, for new BTO contracts, we do not price HDB BTOs to recover construction costs or land costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Certainly, it will cost more as a whole but this is not a factor in determining the price that we set for BTO prices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In any event, in order to manage the overall tender prices for both public and private sectors, I had mentioned earlier in my speech that the agencies are working with the private sector to work on both public and private construction procurement projects going forward.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because what we have seen during this crisis is that contractors are buffering up for uncertainty because they do not know what twists and turns there are in the road ahead, as many of them had found to their detriment in the last year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And, therefore, tender prices, as a whole, for both the public and private sectors, we see an increase.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With such a contract in place, if we can reach an agreement, it will enable contractors to be assured that uncertainty will be cost-shared between the client and the contractor.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we hope that will then provide more assurance to contractors as they bid for new contracts, whether it is a BTO project, whether it is a public sector infrastructure project or whether it is a private sector project.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, all in, to put in clauses in our standard contracts to enable there to be some fair cost-sharing for uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The details will follow as the agencies and our partners reach precise language.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked the Government to consider more measures to help contractors, such as enhancing the Jobs Support Scheme for the sector, further reducing the foreign worker levy and providing additional time for project completion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I have mentioned earlier, we have already intervened significantly and put together a suite of support measures to help the construction industry to cope with the challenges brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will monitor the impact and review if additional support is required as the situation evolves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: BCA will also continue to engage industry stakeholders on their concerns, including on availability of credit that Mr Henry Kwek mentioned.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But all of these are short-term stop-gap measures – foreign worker levy rebates, cost-sharing, grants.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are all measures to help stop the bleed, as I said.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Fundamentally, as I have said repeatedly, both here in this House and also in other settings, we need to work closely with the industry to continue our multi-year effort to transform the sector to become more productive, to grow good local jobs, to reduce overall reliance on low-skilled foreign manpower, for longer term resilience and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And in that regard, I would, in a way, like to thank both Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Leong Mun Wai for supporting the efforts that we have been undertaking since 2017 to push for a holistic transformation of the construction sector, from end-to-end.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim emphasised that by raising the cost of foreign workers, that, in his view, will push employers and contractors to spend more on capital investments to be more productive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Well, we agree with him to an extent but, actually, go a lot further than that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If you look at the Industry Transformation Map (ITM) for the construction sector, both 1.0 and 2.0, since 2017, where we brought developers, contractors, consultants, academics and unionists all together to work on, it is not just the price or the availability of foreign manpower, but ensuring that we digitalise the whole sector, that we put in significant investments in technology, that we fund, grant, support and train our sector, in order to design for manufacturing and assembly, that is, bring into Singapore, into our construction sector, a whole new way of construction that is far more productive, that involves advance precast that can be done off-site.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And I would ask both Members, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim as well as Mr Leong Mun Wai, to look at and read our ITM and tell us whether they fully support it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, during the Committee of Supply (COS) this year, both Minister of State Tan Kiat How and myself took pains to explain again our efforts to transform the sector and create good local jobs for our graduates, for our diploma holders and our ITE certificate holders, in order to push the sector forward.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Leong's point that the Government makes no effort to push productivity in the construction sector, that we do not create local jobs or create opportunities for Singaporeans, befuddles me.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I was just exchanging notes with Minister of State Tan Kiat How because, during COS, that was really the gist of what we were saying.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if the Member would read and re-read Minister of State Tan Kiat How's speech, he gave example after example of Singaporeans who were describing their journey into the construction sector, seeing how the sector has evolved, how technology has created a niche for them, enabled them to build more productively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Old timers who have seen how construction has moved from 2D to 3D using automation; and young entrants, being very excited that the construction sector is becoming far more high-tech, digitalised, connected, interconnected, multi-disciplinary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All this work is happening at great speed but we are pushing hard.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And about productivity, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim felt that productivity in the sector had not improved despite efforts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As a result of the efforts over the many years, both regulatory efforts, for example, when we pushed up the buildability score, builders have to meet with certain buildability score before they are allowed to build GLS sites with preconditions of productivity and methods of construction before you can develop the land.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Regulatory, land-sale related, skills upgrading, grants, grants for individuals, grants for firms and, now, grants for the whole alliance of the value chain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All these are efforts to transform our sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But because the construction sector is a long value chain, it does take time, it does take resolve and no one firm can do it on its own.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And they are bonded to the Singapore firm in order for Singaporeans to be injected into these firms and to grow with these firms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And so, all these are efforts that are publicised, these are efforts that are known that we talk about in this House.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I would invite Mr Leong Mun Wai to come and have a chat with us so we can tell him a bit more about these efforts and we hope he will support them wholeheartedly in growing a strong local core in our construction sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It involves changing mindsets, it involves changing the way firms work, the way firms work with other firms, it involves the Government.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But I think that, at the crux of it today, this Bill, essentially, is about this crisis that we are facing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, yes, in the mid to long term, we will put in a lot of effort, as we have done over the last few years, to transform our construction sector end-to-end.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But in the meantime, what is this House asked to decide at the end of this night?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And that is our sector, construction firms, Singapore firms, construction firms which are faced with a severe manpower crunch, asked to deliver projects, that notwithstanding all the support the Government has given on various fronts that I have articulated, they are short of workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A framework which nudges dialogue and discussion but, beyond which, we put in an adjudicatory framework to ensure that costs are fairly shared.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are abnormal times calling for superhuman efforts to keep Singapore going.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because I recall him saying, "Do not bring in foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Let the contractors take this time during this crisis to learn how to live with less foreign workers." I hope I was mistaken but perhaps the Member could confirm: does he support this Bill?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Does he support the need to help the whole sector during this time?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Does he support the need to alleviate the suffering and pain that the construction sector is under, which will then have knock-on effects on home buyers, property buyers and companies and businesses who are waiting for their properties?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I wanted to address them but I think it may be better if the Member raises a Motion, puts up his ideas, sets out his sums as to how much more ABSD he wants to raise.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And how much does he think it will yield?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And how much will it go in addressing all the strategies that he has set out in his speech earlier?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because he spoke to many contractors who were concerned about the current situation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And does he then support bringing in more foreign workers or does he want to freeze the growth of foreign workers into Singapore?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He said that our approach has to be adaptive and strike a balance between two imperatives: saving lives and protecting livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But, indeed, these are complex, dynamic and fast-changing trade-offs that we have had to consider in managing this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Minister Lawrence Wong explained how the Multi-Ministerial Task Force has sought to steer us through all of this uncertainty in his Ministerial Statement earlier today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Earlier on in my speech and earlier on in the day, during Parliamentary Question Time, I spoke of opening up more non-traditional source countries to recruit foreign workers and I even raised the example of Vietnam because the infection rate there is very low compared to many other ASEAN countries; although, in the last few days, I understand, the numbers are going up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Still, the rise in terms of absolute numbers remains comparatively small.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, that should give an indication about where I stand on the situation affecting some of these companies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My communication has been with the small contractors – those with three, four or five foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And when you lose one or two foreign workers, you cannot execute a project.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But overall, I heard what the Minister said about the ITMs, in particular, the construction ITMs, the longer project, I would say, to wean the sector to be more manpower-lean.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I believe, at some point, the Government will have to present its report card on what its progress has been.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think that will be helpful also for members of the public to make an assessment as to whether the measures, the amount of money put into the ITMs, specifically the construction ITM, to improve productivity has borne fruit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I hope I have answered the Minister's questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I must apologise that I should read the ITMs more from now on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I hope the Minister understands that, as an NCMP, I do not have a lot of resources.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Every day, there are about 50 to 100 pages of materials from Parliament coming into the portal.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am very happy because I hear that Singaporeans are going into the construction industry.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But what the Minister has said just now is about those like managers with scholarships and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For example, how many Singaporeans have come in again to be just a general worker, like substituting those permit workers?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because I believe that when we raise the wages, some of these Singaporeans will come in.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
